assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coupling a superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon in an on-chip resonator, with strong-coupling and dispersive readout, created the architecture on which essentially all superconducting quantum processors and microwave quantum optics now rest. The idea is original, clear and has had lasting impact on quantum technology and on fundamental tests of light-matter interaction in a new regime.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues) are tightly linked. Blais for theory, Schoelkopf and Wallraff for experiment is a workable three-person configuration, but Steven M. Girvin's role in the Yale theory is substantial and the choice between him and Blais is genuinely contestable.
assessment.maturity: Mature: reproduced and extended by many independent groups over two decades, with the transmon and cQED readout now standard in industrial and academic devices. The macroscopic-quantum-circuit line was recognised in 2025, so recognising the architecture that builds on it is timely and coherent.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Girvin over Blais or both with a reduced experimental set; I cannot verify the finer priority questions from memory.
Overlap in subject area with the recent 2025 prize could be viewed as too close by some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological-insulator theory and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall edge states opened a broad field of topological quantum matter, with a new classification of band insulators and robust edge transport. Importance, originality and lasting impact are all high.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and Z2 classification, while Molenkamp's group gave the HgTe quantum-well realisation (with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theory, which is not among the credited names). M. Zahid Hasan's three-dimensional topological-insulator work is a separate part of the compound discovery and would crowd a three-person limit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and three-dimensional materials, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely and arguably somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Credit distribution between the theory of the 2D and 3D cases and between Molenkamp's and other experimental realisations.
The omission of other theory contributors in the supplied credit list makes a fair configuration hard.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and underlies a redefinition of the second and tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The achievement is clear, concrete and of broad scientific and practical importance.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and Ye brought the scheme to the highest precision with strontium clocks and frequency-comb links. The two-person credit is coherent, although the earlier comb and ion-clock work was already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and other clock groups contributed.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with independent confirmation across several national labs and a stable interpretation. Recognition would be timely given the coming redefinition of the second.
uncertainties: Whether a prize here would be judged sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 awards.
Not within my own research expertise, so my assessment rests on general knowledge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum computation with trapped ions and its realisation in entangling gates and digital quantum simulation provided the first scalable-in-principle quantum computing platform and set the template for the field. The concept is original and has shaped quantum-information experiments for three decades.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 proposal, and Blatt's group produced leading experimental realisations. Other ion-trap groups (including NIST and Innsbruck-adjacent efforts) share in the experimental credit, which the three names do not fully cover.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed, with commercial ion-trap processors now operating. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche covered quantum-state control, so some overlap and timing question remains.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the Zoller-Cirac role in the optical-lattice candidate.
Experimental credit among several ion-trap groups is not fully reflected in the three names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising Hubbard-type many-body physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the Mott-insulator transition and quantum-gas microscopy, opened analogue quantum simulation of correlated matter. The impact is lasting and the experiments are clear and original.
assessment.attribution: The experimental credit sits naturally with Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, while Cirac, Zoller and Jaksch supplied the theory framework. Because Cirac and Zoller overlap with the trapped-ion candidate, an experimental-only trio is a defensible but incomplete configuration.
assessment.maturity: Well established with many independent groups, though practical quantum advantage in simulation of open problems is still developing.
uncertainties: Whether theory credit should be included and how that interacts with the trapped-ion candidate.
Frontier of useful quantum simulation is not yet settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the field of moire quantum materials, with strongly correlated physics in a tunable platform. Highly original and influential.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the theoretical prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experimental discovery. The supplied names fit a clean three-person prize, although Cory Dean and others also contributed to the broader moire programme.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across many groups, but the origin of the superconductivity and the broader interpretation remain actively debated, so the field may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of magic-angle superconductivity remains unresolved.
The related fractional Chern and moire discoveries may later require separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault tolerance showed in principle that large quantum computation is possible despite decoherence, and are central to the roadmap of every quantum-computing programme. Conceptual originality and long-term importance are very high, and from my own field I regard error correction as the decisive requirement for useful processors.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane introduced the first quantum codes, while Kitaev contributed topological and fault-tolerant ideas. Gottesman, Calderbank and others, who are not among the credited names, also made decisive contributions, so the configuration is incomplete and contested.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold logical memories are very recent, so confirmation is still developing and the physical-scale payoff has not yet been demonstrated. A prize may be premature.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is better regarded as theoretical computer science than physics.
Credit is spread over more people than the supplied names, and experimental proof of scalable fault tolerance is only emerging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of quantized conductance in ballistic quantum point contacts was a clean, textbook demonstration of Landauer-type transport in mesoscopic systems and underlies the later development of quantum-dot and gate-defined qubit devices. The discovery is clear and foundational, though modest in breadth compared with the leading candidates.
assessment.attribution: The 1988 discovery was made independently by the Delft/Philips group (van Wees, van Houten and co-workers) and the Cambridge group (Wharam, Pepper and co-workers). The supplied names omit D. A. Wharam, which makes a fair attribution doubtful, and Pepper's role in the Cambridge work shares credit with the Cambridge colleagues.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and stable, almost four decades old, so the question is relevance rather than confirmation.
uncertainties: Incomplete credit list and the parallel Delft and Cambridge discoveries.

Whether the committee would view this as sufficiently impactful given that mesoscopic physics has already seen recognition via other prizes. My mesoscopic background may bias me toward this candidate.
